title: Quantification of microstructures in the entorhinal-hippocampus pathway as a sensitive biomarker for neurodegeneration during the preclinical stage of Alzheimer's disease
text:
Once cognitive impairment occurs in an individual with Alzheimer’s disease, it is difficult to modify the devastating
disease process. The long-term goal of this project is to develop a non-invasive tool that can visualize and
quantify microstructural brain changes during the preclinical stage of Alzheimer’s disease. To this end, Dr. Yuto
Uchida will conduct a proof-of-concept study to investigate the feasibility of ultra-high-field quantitative magnetic
resonance imaging as a sensitive biomarker for neurodegeneration in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease.

title: Rare Neurological Disease-Associated Pseudokinases
text:
Proteins called kinases control cell functions by adding phosphate groups to other proteins, but a special subset
known as pseudokinases was thought to be catalytically inactive. However, we have discovered that some
pseudokinases can perform unexpected chemical reactions, and we now aim to investigate whether three
pseudokinases linked to rare neurological diseases—SCYL1, SCYL2, and TBCK—also have enzymatic activity.
By studying these proteins, we hope to uncover new functions that could provide key insights into disease
mechanisms and pave the way for new therapeutic strategies.

title: Targeting cell fusion as a novel strategy to tackle JQ1 resistance in triple negative breast cancer
text:
While JQ1 as an inhibitor of epigenetics showed very promising results in treatment of cancer including
triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), it developed resistance in TNBC. We propose to test a hypothesis
that downregulation of a protein in cell fusion named MFSD2 mediates JQ1-induced cell fusion and drug
resistance. Successful completion of the project will lead to future identification of specific MFSD2
activators as drug candidates to prevent JQ1 resistance in TNBC.

title: Cell intrinsic and extrinsic effects of zinc metabolism in therapy resistant melanoma
text:
The cell cycle regulator p16 is deleted or silenced in ~40% of melanomas, but no current treatment strategies
exist to target this patient population. In this study, we will investigate the role of p16 loss in the resistance to
current standard-of-care therapies though the regulation of zinc homeostasis and whether modulation of extra-
cellular zinc will re-sensitize patients with low p16 expression to current immunotherapies. The results will have
a direct impact on the development of novel therapeutic strategies to obtain a therapeutic response in melanoma
patients with low p16 expression.

title: Operating principles and consequences of T6SS mediated predation in microbial communities
text:
This project defines when and how bacteria use the Type VI secretion system (T6SS), a contact-dependent
weapon, to attack neighbors and harvest nutrients, reshaping environmental and host-associated microbiomes.
We will combine experiments in microfluidics-based structured habitats, automated single-cell time-lapse
imaging, quantitative image analytics, targeted genetics, and comparative metagenomics to map the operational
principles of T6SS. The results will guide strategies to curb pathogens, engineer resilient microbiomes, and
repurpose T6SS as a safe, precision delivery system for therapeutics.

title: Regulation of pancreatic islet cell fate
text:
Significant research efforts are currently underway to understand and prevent the pathogeneses of Type 1 and
Type 2 diabetes, both of which are associated with the gradual loss of functional insulin-producing b cells.
Progress has been made with using human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) populations as alternative sources of
islet cells; however, the efficient production of pure populations of fully functional b cells has not yet been
achieved. This project will use mouse and hPSC models to identify the complex transcriptional and epigenetic
mechanisms that promote the specification and maintenance of islet cell identities.

title: Impact of Obstructive Sleep Apnea and HIV on Ventricular Repolarization Lability
text:
Once regarded as a life-threatening condition, Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection has transformed
into a manageable chronic illness. Recent studies have demonstrated a higher prevalence of obstructive sleep
apnea (OSA) among men living with than without HIV. Epidemiological evidence has also shown that OSA
increases the risk of cardiac complications, such as sudden cardiac death (SCD). The increased risk of SCD in
OSA may be attributed to its impact on ventricular repolarization abnormalities. This study aims to utilize
polysomnographic data from the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study, a longitudinal investigation of HIV, to determine
the independent and interactive effects of OSA and HIV on ventricular repolarization lability.

title: Excessive lipid metabolism in T cell senescence and immunosuppression
text:
The proposed studies address the important issue of immune suppression and dysfunction of tumor-reactive
T cells in the tumor microenvironment that is a major barrier for successful anti-tumor immunity and
immunotherapy. The proposed research has relevance to public health, because it seeks to dissect a novel
suppressive mechanism and then to develop critical strategies that control immune suppression and T cell
dysfunction. Thus, the findings are ultimately expected to be applicable to improve the treatments against
human cancers and other diseases as well.

title: Newborn Iron Deficiency
text:
Iron deficiency is very common nationally and globally during fetal-neonatal life, causes significant
neurobehavioral abnormalities in children (e.g., cognitive and psychosocial deficits), is not reliably prevented by
iron treatment in early life, and results in significant costs to society stemming from lost education/job potential
and increased later developing mental health problems. We propose to perform studies in primary neuron cell
cultures and a dietary rat model of fetal-neonatal iron deficiency anemia to define the specific role of iron
treatment timing and dose in programming brain mitochondrial function and rescuing or exacerbating the long-
term neurobehavioral effects caused by early-life ID. Successful completion of these studies will a) identify a
critical period during pregnancy or early infancy when iron treatment is effective, b) provide mechanistic insights
into how early life iron nutrition programs brain mitochondrial functional capacity across the lifespan and c)
provide a biological foundation for the need for early-life biomarkers of brain iron status to prevent long-term
dysfunction.

title: BCFA Metabolism and the Regulation of Energy Balance
text:
Obesity is a major public health problem that increases the risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and
certain forms of cancer. The studies proposed in this application are designed to understand the role of
peroxisomal metabolism of branched chain fatty acids in activating brown fat-mediated thermogenesis, a
potential strategy to treat obesity.

title: Deep Learning of Renal Scans and Kidney Ultrasounds in Children with Antenatal Hydronephrosis
text:
Obstruction of the flow of urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder can cause increased back pressure on
the kidney that over time can injure the kidney. Currently available imaging techniques are not able to reliably
identify children who are actively experiencing an obstruction. Machine learning can potentially better
determine which patients are experiencing obstruction by identifying features from imaging studies that are not
apparent to human reviewers.

title: Regulation of muscle stem cell dynamics and quiescence
text:
Quiescence is a critical property of adult muscle stem cells, but the mechanisms that underlie this state are
not well understood. We have developed new techniques to study muscle stem cell quiescence, revealing
that these cells are much more dynamic than assumed and that such dynamism is linked to maintenance of
the quiescent state. This proposal aims to identify molecular factors and cellular structures that regulate this
process.

title: Project-004
text: (Overall) This is a program project grant that is centered on improving our understanding of how immune dysregulation can arise and lead to autoimmunity and inflammation. The results of the projects here will help improve our ability to both detect and devise logical treatment strategies for autoimmunity and immune dysregulation.

title: Developmental mechanisms that buffer mutational load in plants
text:
Mutations that accumulate throughout the life cycle can result in cancer, infertility, and aging. This
proposal will characterize how multicellular organisms control genome structure and development in
order to reduce the impact of new mutations, focusing on plant transposons because it is possible to
follow the spread of transposon-mediated mutations soon after they arise. The goal is to establish
general principles that limit the persistence of mutations in diverse species, including humans.

title: Using Ae. aegypti as a model to understand the genomic basis of rapid and repeated evolution
text:
Evolution can drive profound change over millions of years, enabling species to inhabit entirely distinct
ecological niches from their ancestors – but recent results suggest that ecological adaptation can occur much
faster in some cases, across years or even seasons. The proposed research uses repeated transitions
between human-specialist and generalist ecology in the mosquito Aedes aegypti as a model to ask just how
fast ecological differences can evolve, and how. This work uses an integrative combination of field-based
evolutionary genomics, CRISPR-Cas9 analysis of gene function, and experimental evolution to determine the
genomic basis of ecological adaptation, and to analyze the ways that spatial patterns of standing genetic
variation as well as the genomic distribution and effect sizes of adaptive loci shape the rapid evolution of
ecological differences.

title: Cancer Population Science Program
text: The overarching goal of the Cancer Population Science (CPS) Program is to reduce the burden from cancer at a population level. This is achieved through conducting observational, cohort, and interventional studies that focus on primary prevention, early detection, health outcomes, and the delivery of cancer care to varied communities and populations, thereby advancing the HICCC's strategic focus on accelerating innovative clinical and population science research that benefits the Catchment Area and beyond. The CPS Program is co-led by Dawn Hershman, MD, MS, Chin Hur, MD, MPH, and Adana Llanos, PhD, MPH, nationally renowned leaders in their disciplines with durable track records of research and mentorship. The CPS program comprises 50 Members in three schools and 16 departments. In 2024, the 50 CPS Program Members held $16.8M in cancer-focused, peer-reviewed funding (annual direct costs), of which $7.9M (47%) was from NCI, $2.7M (16%) was from other NIH sources, and $6.1M (37%) from other peer-reviewing agencies. During the project period, CPS Program Members authored 780 cancer relevant research publications, of which 236 (30%) were intra-programmatic and 127 (16%) were inter-programmatic. These include 137 (18%) in journals with an impact factor >10, with 62 in journals with impact factors > 20. In addition to leading numerous epidemiologic studies, CPS Program Members lead institutional and multicenter interventional trials, with 1,317 interventional enrollments over the project period, of which 56% were to investigator-initiated trials. The CPS Program, which has research across the human lifespan and cancer control continuum, has four interrelated Specific Aims: (1) Etiology and Primary Prevention - Investigate multi-level cancer risk factors, including socioeconomic determinants of health (SDOH), environmental and lifestyle factors, and underlying genomic susceptibility, that impact lifelong cancer risk in healthy populations to improve primary cancer prevention; (2) Risk Assessment, Screening and Early Detection - Use implementation strategies to integrate molecular-, genomic-, and imaging-based biomarkers into clinical risk assessment and early detection to enhance evidence-based screening; (3) Cancer Care Delivery - Study patterns of cancer care to inform cost-effective treatment, care delivery interventions, and policy initiatives aimed at patients, providers, and health systems; (4) Survivorship and Palliative Care - Discover strategies and translate them to pathway and data-driven trials for patients living with cancer, with a specific focus on symptom management, cancer survivorship, and palliative care. Over the project period, the HICCC has provided support, totaling close to $10M, for recruitments, pilot funding, and resources to foster the growth and development of the CPS Program. Over the next project period we will continue to recruit new faculty based on strategic priorities, develop new initiatives in implementation and dissemination research, continue to lead NCORP and other NCI initiatives, and further cultivate our commitment to the development of trainees and junior faculty.

title: Mach-LETSGO: Machine-LEarning of Treatment, Survey, and Genetics towards Obtaining Correct Classification of Chronic Conditions in Adult Survivors in the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study - CCSS Suppl
text:
Survival rates for many childhood and adolescent cancers have improved at a remarkable pace over the past
five decades. The Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS; U24 CA055727; PI: Armstrong) cohort has been
the source of some of the most significant publications to date addressing the long-term mortality, morbidity and
quality of life of survivors of childhood cancer. Understanding the risk for late effects of childhood cancer and its
therapy provides the basis for health screening recommendations and interventions that can mitigate long-term
health problems in this high-risk population.

title: Multi-Dimensional Sleep Health Predicts Alzheimer’s Markers (DREAM)
text: While a large proportion of Alzheimer’s disease patients report sleep disturbance, clinical trials aimed at improving sleep have been unsuccessful thus far at slowing or preventing cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s Disease burden. This could be due to the fact that sleep dimensions (e.g. sleep duration, sleep disordered breathing) are often studied in isolation, while in clinic sleep is conceptualized as a dynamic process that can be affected in many ways simultaneously. The goal of this K08 is to test the hypotheses that multidimensional sleep health can predict trajectory of cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers in a sample of adults that closely mirror the population of the United States. In addition, we will apply cutting edge machine learning paradigms to examine the association between multidimensional sleep health and accelerated brain aging.

title: Terra-X Upgrade for Siemens Whole Body 7T Terra MRI System
text:
This grant proposal seeks funding to upgrade a whole body 7 Tesla MRI scanner. The
improvements in hardware and software of the scanner aim to address current limitations and
boost ongoing research across numerous NIH-funded projects that investigate various diseases,
including neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, ultimately contributing to better
public health.

title: Intraoperative quantitative CT imaging of breast specimen for reducing re-surgery rate and tumor cataloguing
text:
Breast conserving surgery is used as part of the treatment of breast cancer, the leading cancer among women
in the US, in which the lumpectomy specimen containing breast cancer is excised with a minimum rim of
normal tissue. If the breast cancer close to the specimen edge, referred to as the positive margin, is missed
during the surgery, it can lead to a high rate of re-surgery. We develop an X-ray dual-energy cone-beam
microCT technology for point-care, intraoperative positive-margin identification, allowing for reduction of re-
surgery rate in breast conserving surgery and for tumor cataloguing in breast cancer research and treatment.
